extracted.intended_audience: inventors, in-house counsel, and patent practitioners preparing US design patent drawings or applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on using solid vs. dashed (broken) lines in U.S. design patent drawings — what dashed lines mean, strategic uses to broaden protection, drafting checklist items, and when not to use them (e.g., foreign priority issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of dashed (broken) lines in design patent drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of dashed lines, or broken lines, in design patent drawings means that whatever is drawn in such lines is not claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a US design patent, the claimed design comprises what is drawn in solid lines. The dashed-line feature gives applicants flexibility to show certain parts of a product without claiming those parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid lines define the claimed design
rubrics_metrics.description: In a US design patent the claimed design comprises what is drawn in solid lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing figures, only elements shown in solid lines are part of the claimed design. Use solid lines for features you intend to claim and dashed lines for elements you expressly do not claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dashed lines to show environmental/contextual elements (unclaimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dashed lines enable an applicant to show the environment or context surrounding the claimed design by illustrating, but not claiming, what is external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the product can be attached to, clipped on, hung from or otherwise connected to something else, illustrate that something else in broken lines. Include a broken line statement regarding environmental structure in the specification (see MPEP 1503.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic effect: how dashed lines can broaden protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Dashed lines provide design patent owners with an argument that an accused product infringes even though certain parts of the product look different than what is shown in the design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the visual differences between the accused product and the patented design primarily consist of parts shown in broken lines, and whether the visual similarities are primarily captured by what is shown in solid lines. If so, a dashed-line drafting choice can support an infringement argument focused on the claimed (solid-line) features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist: factors to consider when deciding where to use broken lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical questions to decide which components to show in broken lines rather than claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these factors: Does the product have any functional features or structures that do not contribute to the unique design? Should any external or internal borders be shown in dashed lines? Are there any holes or openings that do not contribute to the unique design? Does the product hold, support, or attach to any external structures that should be shown in broken lines? Would it make sense to reduce the claimed design to a certain component of an overall product or assembly? Is the unique design a two-dimensional graphic artwork placed on a three-dimensional product or article (e.g., GUI)? Is the unique design combined with other features or structures that are not invented by the inventor(s)? Would it make sense to create a new fictional boundary (by using dashed-dot lines) that does not exist in the actual product? Can the product be attached, connected or coupled to something else?

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to include a broken-line statement in the specification for environmental structures
rubrics_metrics.description: If environmental structure is shown in broken lines, include a broken line statement in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP 1503.02 guidance for broken-line statements to explain that depicted environmental elements are not claimed. This supports consistent interpretation during examination and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When not to use dashed lines: foreign priority and international differences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a US design patent application will claim priority to a foreign design application, consider whether the foreign priority application contains any dashed lines; some countries may not allow broken lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each foreign country has its own patent laws which may or may not allow for broken lines in design patents. Introducing broken lines in a US application may affect the priority claim to a foreign priority application that omits broken lines — evaluate priority strategy before adding dashed lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual example / appearance guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines can be used to indicate that the 3-dimensional structure of the product is not being claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to USPTO design patent application guide examples for how broken lines are depicted. Use clear dashed/broken-line conventions so examiners and courts can readily distinguish claimed (solid) from unclaimed (broken) elements. (Source link provided: USPTO design patent application guide.)
